claims.text: Differences in deformation and failure behavior among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloys and their subsets arise primarily from differences in short-range order developed during thermomechanical processing.
Selected elemental combinations promote local chemical ordering and SRO-cluster formation.
SRO clusters act as effective dislocation-pinning centers.
SRO-mediated dislocation pinning and stacking-fault-energy changes enhance strength and alter ductility relative to a fully random equiatomic baseline.
The investigated Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys are single-phase FCC after standardized thermomechanical processing.
Removing one or two elements from equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni can vary the tendency to form SRO.
Identical thermomechanical processing will ensure uniform phase formation and comparable microstructural evolution across the alloys.
SRO clusters formed by local chemical ordering are the structural mediator of the mechanical-property differences.
Favorable elemental interactions promote local SRO.
Local SRO disrupts uniform dislocation motion by providing pinning sites.
SRO-induced pinning and stacking-fault-energy changes increase yield strength and alter work-hardening behavior.
More random atomic distributions contain fewer effective dislocation-pinning centers.
Compositions promoting SRO will have higher yield strength than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Compositions promoting SRO may exhibit improved strain hardening relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Alloys lacking significant SRO will exhibit mechanical behavior similar or inferior to that of the equiatomic quinary baseline.
The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline has a largely random atomic distribution after the specified processing.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase FCC alloys at ambient temperature and typical mechanical-test strain rates and may not apply when secondary phases predominate.
APT or high-resolution TEM can quantify the degree of SRO in these alloys.
